We know this because she says so in her very cool new TV docuseries , which no one asked for, but which Amazon made anyway. I should clarify that Melania: The Series is not to be confused with Melania, the 104-minute-long $75m (£57m) movie Amazon released earlier this year. You know, the one an industry insider called “the most expensive documentary ever made that didn’t involve music licensing”. Various people insinuated nasty things about alleged corruption when that film came out, but I think it’s sweet how patriotic Amazon seems to be. While our cup may runneth over with Melania content, I have good news for first lady fans. We’ve been graced with even more Melania merch. At the weekend, Melania announced an “exclusive collection of digital photographs by internationally acclaimed photographer Ellen von Unwerth” to complement her new docuseries. For the non-refundable price of $150 (£115) you get one black-and-white digital image of the first lady sitting on a chair and one photo in which she is posing next to a clapperboard. The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, despite concerns over his conduct and the supply of AI chips to China, may show that AI – and Huang himself – are ‘too big to fail’. That phrase was on everyone’s lips almost 20 years ago when the Global Financial Crisis struck, and several major banks were bailed out. Given Nvidia’s pivotal role in the AI capex rollout, the implications of Huang’s reinstatement could be profound. Borrowing from the GFC, are some technology CEOs now so systemically important to the future of AI and US leadership in the latest technology revolution that they cannot be fired? Questions around the scale of financing required and future monetisation remain, and the dependence on Huang for the future success of AI may paradoxically heighten those concerns especially given Anthropic fell despite yesterday’s broad market rally. “We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions. stories.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
stories.summary: Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change “as such” the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond Continue reading...

General Trending.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
General Trending.summary: Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change “as such” the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond Continue reading...
